problems.title: First Flight — Find the Lift
problems.mission_briefing: Warm-up. One dial: angle of attack. No camber tricks, no drag budget. Get CL above 0.4.
problems.mission_complete: That's the whole loop — set a parameter, run, read the number. The next one adds a wrinkle.
problems.assumes_you_know: How angle of attack affects lift.
problems.bottleneck: The wing is sitting at α = 0° and making almost no lift (CL ≈ 0). Increase the angle of attack until CL clears 0.4. Nothing else to touch.
problems.hint: Lift rises roughly linearly with angle of attack until stall. Try somewhere around α = 4°.
interview_questions: Run the baseline at α = 0°. What CL do you get?
Raise the angle of attack until CL clears 0.4. What value did it take?

problems.title: Push It Until It Breaks
problems.mission_briefing: Lift went up with angle of attack last time. It doesn't do that forever. Find where it stops.
problems.mission_complete: That collapse is stall — the flow separates off the upper surface and lift falls off while drag spikes. You'll see this shape in every problem from here on.
problems.assumes_you_know: That lift doesn't rise indefinitely with angle of attack.
problems.bottleneck: Sweep angle of attack on the same NACA 0012 well past where it worked last time — somewhere past 16–18°, drag spikes hard as the flow separates. Find an angle where that's unmistakable.
problems.hint: Run a polar sweep from -5° to 20° in one shot instead of testing single points. Watch CD, not just CL — it's the giveaway. Compare it to the CD you saw near α = 4° — it should be many times larger.
interview_questions: Run a polar sweep from -5° to 20°. Where does CL stop climbing?
Look at CD over the same sweep. What happens to it right around where CL peaks?

problems.title: Get the Most Out of It
problems.mission_briefing: Lift alone isn't the job — lift for the least drag is. Find the angle of attack that gets L/D above 80.
problems.mission_complete: L/D is the efficiency number that actually determines range and endurance. There's a best angle for it, and it's not the same angle that maximizes lift.
problems.assumes_you_know: That lift comes at a drag cost.
problems.bottleneck: NACA 2412 at Re = 500,000. At α = 0° it barely produces L/D = 36. Somewhere in the low single digits of angle of attack, efficiency peaks. Find an angle where L/D clears 80.
problems.hint: Run a polar sweep and look for where the L/D curve peaks — it's not at the highest angle of attack you can find.
interview_questions: Run a polar sweep. At what angle of attack does L/D peak?
Is that the same angle where CL is highest? Why or why not?

problems.title: Add Some Curve
problems.mission_briefing: This symmetric section can't hit the lift target no matter the angle of attack you're allowed to use. Change the shape instead.
problems.mission_complete: Camber shifts the whole lift curve upward — more lift at the same angle of attack. It also shifts the pitching moment, which is why cambered wings need a tail to trim.
problems.assumes_you_know: Basic airfoil geometry terms — camber, thickness, chord.
problems.bottleneck: Fixed at α = 4°, Re = 500,000. NACA 0012 (no camber) gives CL ≈ 0.47 — short of the 0.85 target. Angle of attack is off the table. Add camber to the section until CL clears 0.85.
problems.hint: The first digit of a NACA 4-digit code is max camber as % chord. Try stepping it up from 0.
interview_questions: Run the NACA 0012 baseline at α = 4°. How far short of 0.85 is it?
Add camber and re-run. Did the pitching moment change along with CL?

problems.title: Trim the Fat
problems.mission_briefing: Same camber, too thick, too much drag. Get L/D above 80 by changing thickness alone.
problems.mission_complete: Thickness isn't free — more wetted area and more form drag. Once camber is doing its job, thickness is often the next lever, not lift.
problems.assumes_you_know: That geometry affects drag, not just lift.
problems.bottleneck: NACA 2424 at α = 4°, Re = 500,000 gives L/D ≈ 51 — too thick, too much drag. Camber stays the same. Reduce thickness until L/D clears 80.
problems.hint: The last two digits of a NACA 4-digit code are max thickness as % chord. Try stepping it down from 24.
interview_questions: Run the NACA 2424 baseline. How far below 80 is L/D?
Reduce thickness and re-run. How much did L/D move for how much thickness you removed?

problems.title: Same Wing, Different Air
problems.mission_briefing: Same NACA 2412 you've been using. Wrong operating point. Find the Reynolds number where it actually performs.
problems.mission_complete: Same geometry, wildly different performance — that's why quoting a CL or L/D without the Reynolds number is meaningless.
problems.bottleneck: NACA 2412 at α = 4°, Re = 100,000 only manages L/D ≈ 43. The geometry is fine — the operating point is the problem. Try a higher Reynolds number until L/D clears 90.
problems.hint: Say the Reynolds number explicitly when you ask for a run, e.g. "run NACA 2412 at Re 1,000,000" — don't rely on the default.
interview_questions: Run the baseline at Re = 100,000. What's L/D?
Re-run the same geometry at a higher Reynolds number. How much did L/D move without changing the shape at all?

problems.title: UAV Wing — Abrupt Stall
problems.mission_briefing: We lost UAV-7 on the recovery run. Stall at high alpha — no warning, no recovery. Fix the wing before the next flight window or the programme is grounded. Cruise performance must not regress.
problems.mission_complete: UAV-7 cleared its full flight envelope in testing. The stall is now progressive and recoverable. Good work — programme is back on track.
problems.assumes_you_know: How camber and stall interact, and how to read a CL–alpha polar near stall.
problems.bottleneck:
Mission failure: at α = 12° the wing stalls abruptly and the UAV cannot recover — it falls out of the sky. The NACA 2412 at cruise (Re = 500,000, α = 4°) gives CL = 0.8, which is fine, but the sharp stall at high angle of attack makes the aircraft uncontrollable in any gust or manoeuvre that exceeds the cruise point.

Constraint: cruise CL must stay above 0.75. Find a geometry modification that smooths the stall without sacrificing cruise performance.
problems.hint: Increasing camber delays separation — try the 6-series NACA family.
interview_questions: Run a baseline polar sweep and tell me: where does the NACA 2412 stall, and what does the CL curve look like near stall?
What does the shape of that stall curve tell you about the separation behaviour? Is it gradual or abrupt?
Which geometry parameter would you change to soften the stall, and what physical effect are you expecting?
Run the airfoil you have in mind and compare its stall behaviour to the baseline. What changed?
Does your modified airfoil still meet the cruise CL requirement? How do you know?

problems.title: Regional Transport — Symmetric Airfoil Penalty
problems.mission_briefing: The aircraft failed its range certification by 12%. Payload is also under spec. I need a new airfoil section on my desk before the airline review or we lose the contract. Same cruise angle — no changes to the rest of the aircraft.
problems.mission_complete: The airline accepted the revised performance figures. Range and payload targets are met. Contract secured.
problems.assumes_you_know: How camber affects both lift and L/D, and why a symmetric section underperforms at a fixed angle of attack.
problems.bottleneck:
Mission failure: the aircraft cannot reach its destination fully loaded. The NACA 0015 at cruise (Re = 1,500,000, α = 4°) gives L/D = 62 and CL = 0.42 — both short of the targets needed for the required range and payload. The route is marginal even without passengers; with a full load it is impossible.

Constraint: the fix must work at α = 4° without changing the cruise angle of attack. Find the airfoil geometry that closes both gaps at once.
problems.hint: Symmetric airfoils generate less lift per unit drag than cambered ones at the same angle.
interview_questions: Run a baseline on the NACA 0015. Which of the two gaps — L/D or CL — is larger relative to the target?
Why do you think a symmetric airfoil underperforms at a fixed angle of attack? What geometry feature is it missing?
What single geometry change would you expect to close both gaps simultaneously, and why?
Run your candidate airfoil. Did both metrics improve as expected, or did one trade off against the other?
How sensitive is the result to small changes in camber? Use Monte Carlo or compare two nearby candidates.

problems.title: Micro-UAV — Low Reynolds Dual Constraint
problems.mission_briefing: The micro-UAV can't maintain level flight at operating weight. We have one week before the demo. CL is too low and we cannot increase angle of attack — find a geometry that works at the design point or the demo is cancelled.
problems.mission_complete: The UAV completed its full demo flight at operating weight. The client is satisfied. You found a geometry that beats the low-Re physics.
problems.assumes_you_know: How Reynolds number changes which geometry wins, and how to balance two competing targets.
problems.bottleneck:
Mission failure: the UAV cannot sustain level flight at its operating weight. At Re = 100,000 the NACA 0012 produces CL = 0.65 at α = 6° — the wing cannot generate enough lift to carry the aircraft. Increasing angle of attack is not an option; the low-Re flow separates early and L/D collapses.

The mission requires CL > 0.8 (to stay airborne) and L/D > 20 (to meet endurance). These conflict — standard camber increases raise CL but blow up drag at low Reynolds number.

Find the airfoil geometry that satisfies both constraints at Re = 100,000, α = 6°.
problems.hint: At low Reynolds numbers, thin highly-cambered airfoils outperform thick ones — conventional wisdom reverses.
interview_questions: Run the baseline NACA 0012 polar. How does the L/D vs alpha curve differ from what you would expect at Re = 1,000,000?
At Re = 100,000, what happens to the boundary layer that makes thick airfoils less effective?
Your instinct might say more camber helps CL — does adding camber also hurt L/D at this Reynolds number? Test it.
After your first candidate, what surprised you most about the result compared to your prediction?
Run a Monte Carlo on your best candidate. How robust is the performance to small geometry variations at this Reynolds number?

problems.title: Solar UAV — Efficiency-Lift Pareto Problem
problems.mission_briefing: The solar UAV is burning through its energy budget and sagging under sensor load. At current performance the surveillance route is impossible. Find the airfoil that meets both targets — we don't get to pick one, we need both or the mission is scrubbed.
problems.mission_complete: The revised wing met both energy and payload targets in simulation. Mission is viable. The surveillance route is back on the schedule.
problems.assumes_you_know: Everything above — camber, thickness, and Reynolds effects, and how to navigate a two-objective tradeoff.
problems.bottleneck:
Mission failure: the UAV runs out of battery before completing its surveillance route and cannot carry the required sensor payload. At cruise (Re = 600,000, α = 3°, Mach = 0.09) the NACA 2412 gives L/D = 82 and CL = 0.58 — the aircraft burns too much energy and sags under its load. Both targets must be met simultaneously or the mission is scrubbed.

The trap: increasing camber raises CL but adds profile drag, capping L/D. Reducing thickness cuts drag and boosts L/D but limits maximum lift. Every single-parameter change helps one metric while hurting the other.

The design space contains multiple candidates that partially meet the targets — but only certain camber-thickness combinations clear both gaps at once. Find the geometry that lies on the right side of the tradeoff frontier.
problems.hint: Map the L/D vs CL tradeoff across several camber and thickness combinations before narrowing down. The Pareto frontier will show you which candidates dominate.
interview_questions: Run a baseline polar on the NACA 2412. Which of the two targets — L/D or CL — is further from being met at the cruise point?
If you increase camber to fix the CL gap, what do you expect to happen to L/D? Why?
Try a candidate that addresses your primary concern. Did the other metric move in the direction you expected?
You are now navigating a tradeoff. How are you deciding which combinations to test next — what is your search strategy?
Run a Monte Carlo on your best candidate. Does the uncertainty analysis change which geometry you would commit to?
